persons.note: AN 1833 OR 1834 LIST — POLL, TAX OR MUSTER — WITH ANOTHER SOURCE. Read from death_notice, poll_1834. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G2b), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. poll_1834 names this person at Chicago by 31 December 1834 and nothing says when they came. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the person was at Chicago by 1 July 1835 on this record's own evidence. No figure is drawn (L1). OLD SETTLERS, 1879 — A DATE THIS MAN GAVE FOR HIMSELF, AND STILL NOT A FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's FIRST reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, 27 May 1879, printed its register in the proceedings (Early Chicago, Chicago, 1879, pages 84-90), and this man's entry reads “Noble, John, | 1831, June, | Yorkshire, Eng. | 76 | 743 Sedgwick St., Chicago.” — name, his own date of arrival, his birthplace, his age and his 1879 post-office address, in the register's five columns. The date of arrival is HIS RECOLLECTION, set down forty to sixty years after the event; the address is where he lived in 1879 and is never read as an 1835 residence. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 3 times, as “NOBLE JOHN”, 1833-10-22 to 1834-12-25: 1 federal land entry — SW sec 12 T40N R13E and 1 parcel of the school section — lot 5 of block 24 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 320.00 acres stated in all, for $422.50 (ls0294, ls0913, ls0914). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS COOK, UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: NOBLE JOHN matches John Noble: the forename names John Noble of the 4 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

old_settler_deaths.note: LATER EVIDENCE OF A DEATH, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. Fergus's 1843 directory (1896) prints an obituary list of old settlers, and one of its entries meets somebody of this name. THE HEADER OF THE LIST IS QUOTED ABOVE, and it is the limit the whole reading turns on. It does not mean the person was in Chicago in 1835, and it does not mean they arrived before 1843 — the list's own header, quoted above, says it also names citizens who arrived later and others merely 'prominently connected with Illinois history'. A match means one thing: a name in the 1835 layer and a name in this list agree on surname and first initial, and the list gives that name a death date and an age. The date and the interval are the payload. Whatever is carried is carried as evidence of a DEATH and of an interval the birth falls in, never as an 1835 fact and never as a grade. T-0513 consolidates and T-0514/T-0515 apply; this file changes no record. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. A death notice printed in 1896 says a person of this name died on a day; under the ratified ladder (T-0513) that is later evidence about a DEATH, and it is never an 1835 residence. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

people.birth_year_arithmetic: The page prints the death as 'January 13, 1885' and the age as 'aged 82'. An age of 82 completed years means at least 82 and less than 83, so the birth falls between 1802-01-14 and 1803-01-13: the birth year is 1802 or 1803. The subtraction is this project's; the page states no year of birth.

occupation_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints this trade against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Noble, John, real estate, res. Dutchman’s Point'. It is evidence about 1839, written here as 1839's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.
